<reason>CON ran a vivid, well-constructed case (dark patterns, protection "in inverse proportion to vulnerability," the abuser's thumb, entrenchment of first-party platforms) and extracted an honest "Yes, under this rule alone" from PRO. But CON's route to victory depended on treating the motion as a permission slip that "certifies" consensual sales, when the text only prohibits non-consensual ones. PRO's pressure questions exposed this: nothing in the motion overrides a use ban, and CON's own A2 answer ("Yes, it prohibits it") revealed CON wants a stricter rule that logically entails the motion's protection. CON's fallback—that political appetite for harder bans would evaporate and regulators would audit consent logs instead—was plausible but speculative, and PRO correctly labelled it so. PRO also had the cleaner enforceability point: a regulator can check for authorization without proving a buyer's intent, whereas CON's purpose test needs exactly that. CON's argument is largely "do something else instead," which partly swaps the motion; PRO kept the debate on the proposition as written and left the core comparison (silence means no sale vs. sale subject to a purpose test) unneutralized. CON's two clipped rebuttals are a minor execution cost. CON's rhetoric was superior, but PRO's logical spine held, giving PRO a clear but competitive win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The Q1 exchange: PRO asked what in the motion makes consent override a use ban rather than add a condition; CON conceded "Nothing in the motion overrides a use ban" and pivoted to "nothing in the motion contains one." PRO's A4.5/A5.1 then framed CON's minimization as stronger protection that entails, rather than refutes, the motion—CON's "certifies vs. prohibits" reply never fully closed that gap.</best_rebuttal>
